# Trace and audit model

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

If it is not observed, it cannot be audited, debugged, or improved. This
document defines the trace event model, correlation, storage, tamper evidence,
retention, redaction, and the audit queries the factory must answer.

## 2. Trace, audit log, and metrics

| Artifact | Question | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trace | What happened in this run, in order? | Events with parent and correlation IDs |
| Audit log | Who decided what, and why? | Append-only decisions and approvals |
| Metrics | How is the system behaving over time? | Aggregated numbers |

The trace is the detailed record. The audit log is the decision record. Metrics
are derived. A metric without a trace cannot be investigated.

## 3. Event model

Every event has:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `traceID` | The end-to-end correlation ID |
| `spanID` | The event or operation ID |
| `parentSpanID` | The parent operation, when nested |
| `runID` | The run that produced the event |
| `workItemID` | The work item |
| `eventType` | The category |
| `actor` | Role, actor, session, model, policy version |
| `action` | What was attempted |
| `resource` | The target |
| `inputHash` | Hash of the input |
| `outputHash` | Hash of the output |
| `costUSD` | Cost, when known |
| `result` | `ok`, `error`, `denied`, or `blocked` |
| `timestamp` | When it happened |
| `attributes` | Extra key-value data |

Hashes are SHA-256. The event may also carry `previousHash` and `hash` for a
hash chain.

## 4. Event types

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| `session` | Created, resumed, interrupted, completed |
| `tool` | Shell, edit, read, webfetch, MCP call |
| `permission` | Asked, allowed, denied |
| `policy` | Allowed, denied, escalated |
| `evidence` | Produced, verified, invalidated |
| `state` | Transition, checkpoint, terminal state |
| `review` | Finding, decision |
| `acceptance` | Sign-off, revise, block |
| `release` | Gate, canary, rollback |
| `incident` | Opened, contained, resolved |

## 5. Correlation

- One `traceID` spans a work item from intake to observation.
- One `runID` identifies one attempt.
- One `workItemID` links the trace to the issue and the pull request.
- The commit and branch are attributes on the state and release events.
- The parent span links a subagent to its parent.
- A human approval links to the policy decision and the acceptance record.

## 6. Storage and retention

- Append-only storage.
- Access control by role.
- Retention policy per data class.
- Export to JSONL or an observability backend.
- The evidence hash and the trace event are kept even when the artifact is
  external.
- Security and release events are retained longer than transient logs.
- Delete or redact personal data according to policy.

## 7. Tamper evidence

- Hash-chain events, or batch-hash them at a fixed interval.
- Optionally anchor the batch hash in an external transparency log.
- Verify the chain on read and on export.
- A gap or a broken chain is an incident.
- A trace that cannot be trusted cannot support an R3 or R4 acceptance.

## 8. OTel GenAI mapping

An OpenTelemetry exporter maps the trace to spans:

| Mycelia field | OTel GenAI attribute |
| --- | --- |
| model | `gen_ai.request.model` |
| provider | `gen_ai.system` |
| operation | `gen_ai.operation.name` |
| input tokens | `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` |
| output tokens | `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens` |
| tool | span name and attributes |

The mapping is informative. The Mycelia trace schema remains the source of
truth for audit.

## 9. Privacy and redaction

- Never record secrets.
- Redact personal data before export.
- Record the data class on the event when relevant.
- Limit access to traces that contain confidential data.
- Keep the redaction record with the trace.
- Do not put prompt contents in a metric label.

## 10. Audit queries

The trace must answer:

- Who approved this change, and in which role?
- Which model, prompt, policy, and rule versions produced it?
- What evidence was checked, and who verified it?
- What did the run cost?
- Which tool calls were denied or blocked?
- Which exceptions are active, and when do they expire?
- What was the exact sequence for this run?
- Which human decisions were made, and on what evidence?

## 11. Failure handling

- If the trace store is unavailable, buffer locally and alert.
- If the buffer is full, stop the run rather than lose the audit.
- If a gap is detected, mark the trace unproven and stop R3/R4 work.
- If the chain is broken, open an incident.
- Never continue silently without an audit trail.

## 12. Evidence

- Trace export with a hash.
- Integrity check result.
- Retention record.
- Redaction record.
- Audit query result for the sampled runs.

## 13. Anti-patterns

- Logs only at the end of a run.
- No correlation ID.
- Mutable logs.
- Secrets or personal data in logs.
- Infinite retention with no access control.
- Metrics with no trace.
- A trace with no evidence links.
- An audit query that cannot be answered.
- Continuing after an audit gap.

## 14. Data contract

- Schema: [schemas/trace-event.schema.json](../../schemas/trace-event.schema.json)
- Example: [examples/trace-event.example.yaml](../../examples/trace-event.example.yaml)

# Economics

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

Autonomy that is not economically sustainable is not autonomy. This document
defines the cost model, the unit economics, attribution, budgeting, the cost
levers, and the return on investment.

## 2. Cost categories

| Category | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Model tokens | Input, output, cache read and write |
| Compute | Agent runtime, sandbox, build, test |
| CI minutes | Runner time, concurrency |
| Storage | Artifacts, traces, evidence |
| Human time | Review, acceptance, incident, policy |
| Incidents | Rollback, recovery, lost work |
| Tooling | Licenses, managed services |

A cost model that counts only tokens is not a cost model.

## 3. Unit economics

| Metric | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Total cost | Tokens + compute + CI + storage + human + incidents |
| Cost per accepted change | Total cost divided by accepted changes |
| Cost per attempt | Total cost divided by attempts |
| Rework cost | Cost of rejected and revised runs |
| Cost per risk tier | Total cost for the tier divided by accepted changes in the tier |
| Human cost | Review minutes multiplied by the loaded hourly rate |
| ROI | Value delivered divided by total cost |
| Payback | Cost divided by monthly value |
| Autonomy value | Human minutes saved minus review, audit, and incident cost |

## 4. Attribution

Every cost record carries:

- work item
- role
- run and session
- model and provider
- repository and team
- risk tier
- timestamp

Attribution comes from usage events, the trace, and the cost record. A cost
without attribution cannot be managed or charged back.

## 5. Budgeting

- Per run, per day, and per month.
- Reserve a share for rollback and incident response.
- Alert at 50, 80, and 100 percent.
- Stop at the limit; do not retry on a new budget without a decision.
- Review the budget against the value and the risk tier.
- A budget that is never reached may be too high; a budget that is always
  reached may be a capacity problem.

## 6. Cost levers

- Route low-risk work to a cheaper model.
- Use prompt caching and batch requests.
- Keep the context small and relevant.
- Reduce unnecessary tool calls.
- Cache dependencies in CI.
- Use the smallest sandbox that meets the isolation requirement.
- Parallelize independent work.

Do not cut verification to reduce cost. The rework and incident cost is
usually larger.

## 7. Human cost

Human cost includes:

- review and acceptance time
- context switching
- approval queue waiting
- incident command
- policy and exception maintenance

A fast agent with a slow review queue is not a fast factory. Measure the queue
time, not only the run time.

## 8. ROI and value

Value can be:

- revenue from faster delivery
- cost avoidance from fewer incidents
- risk reduction from better evidence
- cycle time reduction
- quality improvement
- human time freed for higher-value work

Measure before and after. Include rework, incidents, and human time. An ROI
without a baseline is a guess.

## 9. Chargeback and showback

- Start with showback: report cost by team and work item.
- Move to chargeback when the attribution is stable.
- Allocate shared costs: runtime, CI, trace storage, human review.
- Review the allocation quarterly.
- Do not charge a team for a shared incident caused by the platform.

## 10. Capacity planning

- Estimate demand: work items per week by risk tier.
- Measure concurrency and queue time.
- Use the WIP limit and Little's law to size the system.
- Plan capacity for review and incident response, not only for agents.
- Revisit after a model or tool change.

## 11. Worked example

Illustrative numbers:

- 100 runs, 60 accepted.
- Model and compute: 1,200 USD.
- Human review: 10 hours at 50 USD per hour = 500 USD.
- Total: 1,700 USD.
- Cost per accepted change: 1,700 / 60 = 28.33 USD.

Compare with the baseline cost per change and the value delivered. The number
is only meaningful next to the baseline.

## 12. Anti-patterns

- Counting tokens but not human time.
- Ignoring rework and incidents.
- Cost per run without accepted changes.
- No attribution.
- Cutting verification to save money.
- A budget with no reserve.
- ROI with no baseline.
- Chargeback before the attribution is stable.

# Evaluation and model change

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

A model or prompt change without an evaluation is a hope, not a decision. This
document defines the evaluation suite, the metrics, and the change process for
models, prompts, policies, and agent profiles.

## 2. What to evaluate

| Dimension | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Task success | Does the agent complete the work item? |
| Quality | Is the result correct, readable, and reversible? |
| Safety | Does it respect policy, secrets, and scope? |
| Evidence | Does it produce the required evidence? |
| Cost | Is the cost within the budget? |
| Latency | Is the feedback loop fast enough? |
| Tool use | Does it choose and call tools correctly? |

## 3. Evaluation suite

| Suite | Purpose | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke | Fast check on every change | 3-5 tasks |
| Golden | Representative work items | 10-50 tasks |
| Regression | Every escaped defect becomes a task | Growing |
| Adversarial | Prompt injection, policy bypass, secret access | 10-30 cases |
| Held-out | Optional, not visible to the agent | Small |

Task sources:

- real work items with acceptance criteria
- incidents and escaped defects
- synthetic tasks for edge cases
- adversarial cases from the threat model

Each task has a fixed input, an expected outcome, and a scoring method.

## 4. Metrics

| Metric | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| pass@1 | The task passes on the first attempt |
| pass@k | The task passes within k attempts |
| rubric score | The review rubric result |
| evidence completeness | Required evidence present and verified |
| policy violations | Denied or blocked actions |
| cost | Cost per task |
| latency | Time per task |
| human intervention | Runs that need a human decision |

Thresholds:

- no regression on safety or policy
- pass rate within the agreed tolerance of the baseline
- cost within the agreed budget
- no new critical finding

## 5. Change process

1. **Define the subject.** Model, prompt, policy, or agent profile, with a
   version.
2. **Record the baseline.** The current version's metrics.
3. **Run the suite.** Smoke, golden, regression, and adversarial.
4. **Compare.** Pass rate, safety, evidence, cost, and latency.
5. **Decide.** Adopt, canary, reject, or roll back.
6. **Canary.** Run on low-risk work for a limited period.
7. **Roll out.** Expand only when the canary is stable.
8. **Monitor.** Watch the health metrics and the error budget.
9. **Roll back.** Revert to the baseline on a regression.

A model change without a baseline is not an evaluation.

## 6. Model routing

- Route low-risk work to a cheaper model when the evaluation supports it.
- Route R3 and R4 to a model with a current evaluation.
- Define a fallback for provider outages.
- Record the route in the trace.
- Do not route R3 or R4 to a model that has not passed the suite.
- Re-evaluate when the provider changes a model or a default.

## 7. Prompt and policy changes

A prompt or policy change follows the same process:

- version the change
- run the smoke, golden, and adversarial suites
- canary on low-risk work
- record the decision
- keep the previous version for rollback

A policy change that tightens access does not need a canary, but it needs a
negative test.

## 8. Evaluation record

The record contains:

- the suite and its version
- the subject type, ID, and version
- the baseline and its score
- the result: score, pass rate, cost, latency, regressions
- the decision: adopt, canary, reject, or rollback
- the timestamp

## 9. Anti-patterns

- Changing a model because it feels better.
- No baseline.
- A suite that never grows.
- A suite the agent can see and optimize for.
- A canary with no metric.
- A rollback path that was never tested.
- R3 or R4 on an unevaluated model.
- A prompt change with no version.

## 10. Data contract

- Schema: [schemas/evaluation-record.schema.json](../../schemas/evaluation-record.schema.json)
- Example: [examples/evaluation-record.example.yaml](../../examples/evaluation-record.example.yaml)

# Incident response

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

Autonomy changes the incident surface. An agent can leak a secret, weaken a
test, merge a bad change, or exhaust a budget faster than a human. The factory
needs a practiced response, not an improvised one.

## 2. Severity

| Severity | Criteria | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEV1 | Active data loss, secret exposure, security breach, or full outage | Immediate; incident commander; all hands |
| SEV2 | Major degradation, contained security issue, or a release that must be rolled back | Within the hour |
| SEV3 | Limited impact, one repository or one role, workaround exists | Same day |
| SEV4 | Near miss or no impact | Next business day |

Severity can rise as information arrives. It rarely falls without evidence.

## 3. Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Incident commander | Owns the response and the decisions |
| Operations lead | Runs containment and recovery |
| Security lead | Leads security investigation |
| Communications lead | Internal and external updates |
| Scribe | Timeline, actions, and evidence |
| Subject-matter expert | Repairs the specific system |

One person may hold several roles in a small team. The commander is always a
human.

## 4. Lifecycle

```text
detect -> triage -> contain -> eradicate -> recover -> postmortem
```

Each step records a timestamp, an owner, and the evidence.

- **Detect.** Alert, report, or audit finding.
- **Triage.** Assign severity, commander, and roles.
- **Contain.** Stop the spread: kill switch, revoke credentials, quarantine a
  component, roll back a release.
- **Eradicate.** Remove the cause.
- **Recover.** Restore service and verify.
- **Postmortem.** Learn and change the system.

## 5. Playbooks

### Prompt injection or policy bypass

- Stop the session.
- Preserve the trace.
- Identify the source: repo, issue, web, MCP, or tool.
- Quarantine the source.
- Add a regression test and a policy rule.

### Secret leak

- Revoke and rotate the secret.
- Audit its use.
- Remove it from logs and traces.
- Notify the owner.
- Add a secret-scan test.

### Malicious MCP server, plugin, or skill

- Disable the component.
- Remove it from the allowlist.
- Rotate credentials.
- Review other repositories that used it.
- Add a supply-chain check.

### Runaway agent or budget exhaustion

- Trigger the kill switch.
- Interrupt the session.
- Revoke the credentials.
- Preserve the trace.
- Lower the budget or the autonomy ceiling.

### Bad release

- Stop the rollout.
- Roll back to the previous artifact.
- Disable the feature flag.
- Verify the recovery.
- Record the release and rollback.

### Data corruption

- Stop writes.
- Restore from the tested backup or run the down migration.
- Reconcile the data.
- Verify the invariants.
- Record the recovery.

### Trace gap

- Stop high-risk work.
- Restore the trace from the buffer or backup.
- Mark the affected runs unproven.
- Re-run the evidence if possible.
- Record the gap.

## 6. Kill switch and break-glass

- The kill switch stops the run, revokes credentials, disables the component,
  and preserves the trace.
- Break-glass is time-bound, owned, and recorded.
- Break-glass cannot disable the trace or the evidence requirement for R3/R4.
- The post-incident review happens before the next release.

## 7. Communication

- Use one internal channel and one status owner.
- Update at a fixed cadence until resolved.
- State what is known, what is not known, and when the next update will be.
- Do not speculate about cause or blame.
- External communication for a security or data incident goes through the
  owner and legal review.

## 8. Postmortem

A postmortem is blameless and evidence-based:

- timeline
- impact
- root cause and contributing factors
- detection and response
- what worked and what did not
- actions with owners and due dates

A postmortem without an action is incomplete.

## 9. Feedback

Every incident updates at least one of:

- a policy or permission rule
- a regression test
- an evaluation task
- a runbook
- the threat model
- the concern radar
- the readiness assessment

## 10. Incident record

The record contains:

- severity and category
- status
- commander
- detection time
- summary
- containment
- postmortem link
- actions with owners and due dates
- trace reference

## 11. Anti-patterns

- No incident commander.
- Blame instead of system change.
- No timeline.
- No containment before root cause.
- No postmortem.
- A postmortem with no action.
- Ignoring a near miss.
- Disabling the trace to "move faster".
- External communication without review.

# Rule lifecycle

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

Rules rot. Without an owner, a version, a test, and a retirement path, the
control plane becomes a museum of stale constraints. This document defines the
lifecycle of a rule and the registry that keeps it honest.

## 2. Rule types

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Policy | Deny a shell command, provider, or MCP server |
| Permission | Allow a role to edit a path or run a test |
| Evidence requirement | Require mutation or review for a risk tier |
| Review threshold | Minimum mutation score or coverage |
| Role contract | Allowed and denied actions for a role |
| Budget | Token, cost, time, or concurrency limit |
| Model routing | Model by risk tier or cost |

## 3. Rule record

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable rule identifier |
| `title` | Short description |
| `owner` | Person or role accountable |
| `version` | Semantic version |
| `status` | Draft, active, deprecated, retired |
| `rationale` | Why the rule exists |
| `scope` | Repositories, roles, risk tiers |
| `effectiveAt` | When it becomes active |
| `reviewAt` | When it must be reviewed |
| `evidence` | What proves compliance |
| `tests` | Positive and negative tests |
| `exceptions` | Active exceptions |
| `supersedes` | Rule or version it replaces |

## 4. Lifecycle

| State | Meaning | Enforced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Draft | Proposed, under review | No |
| Active | Approved and enforced | Yes |
| Deprecated | Still enforced, removal scheduled | Yes |
| Retired | Removed from the runtime | No |

A rule moves forward one state at a time. A rule cannot be retired while an
active exception depends on it.

## 5. Change process

1. Open an issue with the rule and the reason.
2. Write the rule record and the tests.
3. Open a draft pull request.
4. Review the rule, the tests, and the migration.
5. Canary the change where possible.
6. Activate the rule and update the registry.
7. Announce the change to the adopters.

A rule change follows the same review and CI process as any other normative
change.

## 6. Precedence and conflicts

- The stricter rule wins.
- OpenCode policy precedence is managed, system, Console, global, project.
- A project cannot re-enable what a higher authority denied.
- A conflict that cannot be resolved by precedence leaves the work item
  `blocked`.
- A duplicate rule is consolidated, not left to drift.

## 7. Exceptions

An exception is a time-bound, owned deviation:

- names the rule and the scope
- names the owner and the justification
- names the compensating control
- has an expiry and a review date
- is visible in the trace and the readiness report
- cannot disable a red line
- is renewed only with a new review

A permanent exception is a rule change in disguise.

## 8. Testing

- Every rule has a positive test: the allowed action proceeds.
- Every rule has a negative test: the denied action is blocked.
- A threshold rule has a boundary test.
- A policy change runs a dry run against historical decisions.
- The tests are part of the pull request evidence.

## 9. Deprecation and retirement

- Announce the deprecation at least one minor release before removal.
- Name the replacement or the reason for removal.
- Keep the rule enforced until the removal date.
- Remove the rule and update the registry.
- Record the retirement in the release notes.
- A retired rule cannot be silently reintroduced; it needs a new record.

## 10. Rule registry

The registry lists:

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Rule ID | `RULE-001` |
| Version | `1.2.0` |
| Status | `active` |
| Owner | `security-owner` |
| Review date | `2027-01-31` |
| Replacement | `RULE-014` |

The planned location is `rules.yaml` or a section of `mycelia.yaml`. Until the
schema exists, the registry is a table in the readiness report.

## 11. Metrics

- active rules by type
- active exceptions and expired exceptions
- overdue reviews
- rule violations
- rule age
- rules retired per release

## 12. Anti-patterns

- An orphan rule with no owner.
- A rule with no test.
- A permanent exception.
- Duplicate or conflicting rules.
- A threshold that is never reviewed.
- A deprecation with no replacement or date.
- A retired rule that reappears without a record.
- A registry that is not updated.

# Template and adoption boundary

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

Adoption fails when a team forks the core or when every local change becomes a
permanent divergence. This document defines the shared core, the profile, the
local layer, the `mycelia.yaml` root config, and the conformance claim.

## 2. Three layers

| Layer | Owner | Examples | Change process |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Core | Mycelia maintainer | Normative specs, schemas, default profile, assessment | Issue and reviewed pull request |
| Profile | Mycelia maintainer | Minimal, standard, high-assurance | Core process |
| Local | Adopter | Commands, owners, budgets, providers, exceptions | Adopter's process |

The local layer may narrow the core; it may not weaken a red line. A local
override that conflicts with the core is invalid.

## 3. Core

- the normative specification
- the JSON Schemas
- the default OpenCode profile
- the readiness assessment
- the commands and skills
- the conformance tests

The core is versioned and copied. It is not forked.

## 4. Profile

A profile selects a set of controls and thresholds:

| Profile | Target | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal | L1 | Work item, role, policy, evidence, terminal states |
| Standard | L2 | Minimal plus sandbox, independent review, sampling, trace |
| High-assurance | L3-L4 | Standard plus provenance, mutation, incidents, evals, assessment |

A profile inherits the lower profiles.

## 5. Local

The adopter configures:

- repository name and owner
- commands and test entry points
- risk-tier examples for the repository
- budgets and concurrency
- providers and models
- trace sink and retention
- owners and escalation
- time-bound exceptions
- adapters for the Git provider and CI

The local layer is declared in `mycelia.yaml`.

## 6. `mycelia.yaml`

The root configuration declares:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `profile` | Minimal, standard, or high-assurance |
| `autonomy.ceiling` | The highest level the repository may run at |
| `autonomy.default` | The default level for a new work item |
| `runtime` | OpenCode version and config path |
| `riskTiers` | Repository examples for R0-R4 |
| `evidenceManifest` | Path to the manifest |
| `roles` | Enabled roles |
| `policies` | Policy bundles |
| `budgets` | Cost, token, step, and concurrency limits |
| `observability` | Trace sink and retention |
| `dataClasses` | Allowed data classes |

## 7. Distribution

- Copy the template, do not fork the core.
- Pin the core version in `mycelia.yaml`.
- Keep local changes in the local layer.
- Upgrade by diffing the new template against the old, not by overwriting the
  adopter's configuration.
- Record the upgrade in the release notes.
- Run the conformance tests after the upgrade.

## 8. Precedence

- The core red lines cannot be weakened.
- The profile sets defaults; the local layer may tighten them.
- The stricter rule wins.
- OpenCode policy precedence is managed, system, Console, global, project.
- A local override that cannot be reconciled leaves the work item `blocked`.

## 9. Conformance claims

An adopter may claim:

- the profile it implements
- the autonomy ceiling with evidence
- the controls it has adopted
- the deviations and exceptions

An adopter may not claim:

- certification by Mycelia
- a level above its assessed ceiling
- a control it has not evidenced
- another harness's conformance

The readiness report is the evidence for the claim.

## 10. Golden path

1. Copy the template.
2. Fill `mycelia.yaml`.
3. Run the readiness assessment.
4. Fix the blocking gaps.
5. Run one low-risk change through the loop.
6. Raise the level only with evidence.

## 11. Anti-patterns

- Forking the core.
- Editing the core in place.
- A local override that weakens a red line.
- A conformance claim with no evidence.
- A template upgrade that overwrites local configuration.
- A profile with no owner.
- An exception that never expires.

- Schema: [schemas/mycelia.schema.json](../../schemas/mycelia.schema.json)
- Example: [examples/mycelia.example.yaml](../../examples/mycelia.example.yaml)

# Adoption guide

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

The specification is only useful if a team can adopt it without a big-bang
rewrite. This guide defines the greenfield and brownfield paths, the phases,
the entry and exit criteria, and the evidence for each step.

## 2. Prerequisites

- a named human owner
- access to the repository and CI
- authority to change branch protection and permissions
- a pilot repository or service
- a security owner for R3 and R4
- a rollback path for anything already in production

## 3. Minimal viable adoption

1. Add a work item with a goal, acceptance criteria, risk tier, and evidence.
2. Add a role contract and a policy with red lines.
3. Add canonical checks that run from a clean clone.
4. Add an evidence manifest for R0 and R1.
5. Use the draft-first pull request flow and forbid direct pushes to `main`.

This is enough for L1. Do not wait for the full profile.

## 4. Greenfield

1. Create the repository from the template.
2. Fill `mycelia.yaml`.
3. Copy `opencode.json` and `.opencode/`.
4. Add the CI checks and the evidence manifest.
5. Run the readiness assessment.
6. Run one R0 change through the full loop.
7. Raise the level only with evidence.

## 5. Brownfield

1. Pick a pilot repository or service.
2. Run the baseline assessment; record the ceiling.
3. Make the repository legible: README, commands, pinned toolchain, ownership.
4. Make the checks deterministic; quarantine flaky tests with an owner.
5. Add `AGENTS.md` and the role contracts.
6. Add the policy red lines and the evidence manifest.
7. Add the sandbox, budgets, and kill switch.
8. Add independent review and acceptance sampling.
9. Add trace and provenance.
10. Reassess and promote one level at a time.

Start with R0 and R1 work. Do not start with the riskiest change in the
repository.

## 6. Phases

| Phase | Entry | Exit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 Baseline | Access and owner | Readiness report with ceiling |
| 1 Legibility | Baseline | Clean clone runs the checks |
| 2 Feedback | Legibility | CI green; flake rate bounded |
| 3 Control | Feedback | Roles, policy, evidence, decision rights |
| 4 Containment | Control | Sandbox, budgets, kill switch |
| 5 Assurance | Containment | Independent review, mutation, acceptance |
| 6 Observability | Assurance | Trace, provenance, metrics |
| 7 Promotion | All phases | Readiness report meets the target; drills pass |

Every phase has an owner and evidence. A phase without evidence is not
complete.

## 7. Roles

| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Human owner | Owns the adoption and the risk |
| Platform engineer | Builds the runtime, CI, sandbox, and trace sink |
| Security owner | Reviews the policy, secrets, and R4 changes |
| Maintainer | Keeps the local profile and the evidence current |
| Pilot team | Runs the first changes and reports friction |

## 8. Evidence per phase

- Baseline: readiness report, ceiling, gap register.
- Legibility: clean-clone log, command list, ownership record.
- Feedback: CI result, flake rate, check time.
- Control: role contracts, policy tests, evidence manifest.
- Containment: sandbox config, budget test, kill-switch drill.
- Assurance: review record, mutation report, acceptance sample.
- Observability: trace export, provenance record, metrics.
- Promotion: readiness report, canary result, human approval.

## 9. Common blockers

| Blocker | Remedy |
| --- | --- |
| Flaky tests | Quarantine with an owner and an expiry; do not retry to pass |
| No CI | Start with lint, link check, and schema validation |
| No owner | Assign one before starting |
| Monorepo ambiguity | Add per-package commands and ownership |
| Secrets in the environment | Move to a broker; deny `.env` |
| Approval fatigue | Sample by risk; raise the evidence quality |
| Legacy release | Add a rollback and a canary before changing the release |
| No test suite | Add characterization tests before refactoring |

## 10. Upgrade

- Reassess after each phase.
- Read the new template diff; do not overwrite local configuration.
- Run the conformance tests.
- Record the upgrade and the new ceiling.
- Announce the change to the pilot team.

## 11. Anti-patterns

- A big-bang adoption.
- Buying a better model instead of fixing the repository.
- Skipping the baseline.
- Starting with an over-permissioned pilot.
- No human owner.
- No rollback.
- Claiming a level without evidence.
- Copying the normative specs into the adopter.

# Assurance case

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

An assurance case states a claim, argues why it is true, and shows the evidence.
This document is the top-level case for Mycelia: it connects the claims to the
specification and the evidence.

The structure follows the claims-arguments-evidence pattern used by Goal
Structuring Notation (GSN). It is informative, not a formal proof.

## 2. Claim hierarchy

**C1.** For a repository assessed at level Lx, the factory constrains authority,
bounds execution, produces trustworthy evidence, and recovers from failure.

| Subclaim | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| C1.1 | Authority is bounded by roles, policy, and isolation. |
| C1.2 | Work is well-formed by intake and context. |
| C1.3 | Execution is bounded, durable, and recoverable. |
| C1.4 | Evidence is trustworthy and independently verified. |
| C1.5 | Operations are observable and incidents are recoverable. |
| C1.6 | The system evolves only through evaluated change. |

## 3. Arguments and evidence

| Claim | Argument | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C1.1 | Roles limit actions; policies deny red lines; the sandbox contains the process | Role contract, policy decision, negative test, sandbox test |
| C1.2 | The work item defines the goal and the evidence; context is assembled and refreshed | Work item, context manifest, readiness report |
| C1.3 | The loop has gates, checkpoints, budgets, and terminal states | Run state, resume test, kill-switch drill |
| C1.4 | The manifest defines done; mutation protects tests; review and acceptance are independent | Evidence manifest, test integrity report, review record, acceptance record |
| C1.5 | Every action is traced; provenance links artifacts; incidents have a playbook | Trace export, provenance record, incident record |
| C1.6 | Model, prompt, and policy changes pass an evaluation; rules have a lifecycle | Evaluation record, rule registry, readiness report |

## 4. GSN-style view

```text
C1 Factory safe at Lx
├── C1.1 Authority bounded
│   ├── A1 Role contracts limit actions
│   ├── A2 Policies deny red lines
│   └── E1 Negative policy and sandbox tests
├── C1.2 Work well-formed
│   ├── A3 Work item defines done
│   ├── A4 Context is assembled and fresh
│   └── E2 Work item and context evidence
├── C1.3 Execution bounded
│   ├── A5 State machine with gates
│   ├── A6 Budgets and stop conditions
│   └── E3 Run state and drills
├── C1.4 Evidence trustworthy
│   ├── A7 Manifest and verification
│   ├── A8 Test integrity
│   ├── A9 Independent review
│   └── E4 Integrity, review, acceptance
├── C1.5 Operations observable
│   ├── A10 Trace and provenance
│   ├── A11 Incident response
│   └── E5 Trace, provenance, incident
└── C1.6 Evolution controlled
    ├── A12 Evaluations
    ├── A13 Rule lifecycle
    └── E6 Evaluation, registry, readiness
```

## 5. Assurance deficits

The case is only as strong as its evidence. Known deficits:

- The specification is not a certification.
- The controls depend on the implementation, not only on the document.
- Human factors, such as approval fatigue, are mitigated but not eliminated.
- The model provider is a trust boundary outside the factory.
- Model behavior can change without a version change.
- Evidence can be stale or incomplete.
- The external framework mapping is informative.
- No formal proof is claimed.

Each deficit is either accepted with a rationale or tracked as a gap.

## 6. Review

Review the assurance case:

- before an L3 or L4 promotion
- quarterly
- after an incident
- after a model, provider, or policy change
- after a framework or standard change

The review records the claims checked, the evidence sampled, the deficits
accepted, and the actions.

# Conformance profiles

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

An adopter needs a clear target and a claim they can defend with evidence.
This document defines the Minimal, Standard, and High-assurance profiles, the
conformance claim, and the selection rules.

## 2. Profiles

| Profile | Target level | Human role | Allowed risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal | L1 | Merges every change | R0-R2 with review |
| Standard | L2 | Accepts by sampling | R0-R2; R3/R4 human |
| High-assurance | L3-L4 | Policy, high risk, audit | R0-R2 unattended; R3/R4 human |

A profile inherits the profiles before it.

## 3. Profile requirements

### Minimal

Required controls at 2 or higher:

- `CTL-01` to `CTL-04`
- `CTL-07`, `CTL-08`
- `CTL-10` to `CTL-14`

The repository has a work item, a role contract, a policy, an evidence
manifest, and terminal states. A human runs the checks and merges.

### Standard

Minimal plus these controls at 2 or higher:

- `CTL-05`, `CTL-06`, `CTL-09`
- `CTL-15` to `CTL-17`
- `CTL-19`, `CTL-21`

The repository has a sandbox, an independent reviewer, acceptance sampling, a
trace, a merge queue, and a tested rollback. A human accepts by sampling.

### High-assurance

Standard plus these controls at 3 or higher:

- `CTL-20`, `CTL-22`, `CTL-23`, `CTL-24`

For L4, `CTL-15`, `CTL-16`, `CTL-17`, `CTL-23`, and `CTL-24` must be at 3 or
higher, and the incident and concurrency drills must pass.

The repository has mutation testing, provenance, incident drills, and an
evaluation suite. A human owns policy, high risk, and audit.

## 4. Conformance claim

A claim names:

- the profile and level
- the commit assessed
- the readiness report
- the evidence sampled
- the deviations and exceptions
- the date

Example:

> Conformant to Mycelia Standard at L2, assessed at commit `abc123`, report
> `RPT-001`, on 2026-11-13. No active exceptions.

A claim is invalid when:

- the report is expired
- a blocker is open
- a control lacks evidence
- the repository changed materially since the assessment

## 5. Selection, upgrade, and downgrade

- Start at Minimal.
- Move to Standard after an L2 assessment.
- Move to High-assurance before targeting L3 or L4.
- A repository may run below its profile; it may not run above it.
- Downgrade after an incident, a failed assessment, or a policy change.
- Record the change in the readiness report and the release notes.

## 6. Profile matrix

| Capability | Minimal | Standard | High-assurance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work item and evidence | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Role and policy | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Sandbox | Recommended | Required | Required |
| Independent review | Recommended | Required | Required |
| Acceptance sampling | No | Required | Required |
| Trace | Basic | Required | Required |
| Merge queue | No | Required | Required |
| Mutation testing | No | Recommended | Required |
| Provenance | No | Recommended | Required |
| Incident drills | No | Recommended | Required |
| Evaluations | No | Recommended | Required |
| Autonomy ceiling | L1 | L2 | L3-L4 |

## 7. Inheritance

A profile inherits every requirement of the profiles before it. A higher
profile cannot waive a lower-profile requirement; it can only add controls.

## 8. Assessment mapping

The readiness assessment produces the score and the ceiling. The profile is
the target; the ceiling is the safe maximum. The claim is valid only when the
ceiling is at or above the profile's target level.

## 9. Anti-patterns

- Claiming High-assurance without the evidence.
- Using a profile as a badge.
- Skipping Minimal and Standard.
- Mixing profiles per work item without a rule.
- Claiming conformance for another harness.
- A claim with an expired report.
- A profile with no owner.

Status: Draft

# OpenCode conformance checklist

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

The runtime contract needs a runnable checklist so an adopter can verify the
OpenCode setup instead of assuming it. This checklist is the practical form of
[opencode-runtime-contract.md](../30-execution/opencode-runtime-contract.md).

## 2. How to use

Run the checks in a disposable clone or a sandbox. Record the version, the
commit, and the result. A failed check is a gap, not a warning.

## 3. Checklist

| ID | Check | Method | Pass criterion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OC-01` | Version | `opencode --version` | 2.2.6 or newer |
| `OC-02` | Config schema | Validate `opencode.json` | Schema validation passes |
| `OC-03` | Default agent | Read `default_agent` | The agent exists and is primary |
| `OC-04` | Custom agents | `opencode api get /api/agent` | Every role is listed |
| `OC-05` | Commands and skills | `opencode api get /api/command` and `/api/skill` | Every command and skill is listed |
| `OC-06` | Base permissions | Read the effective permissions | No broad `* allow` remains |
| `OC-07` | Red lines | Read the effective policies | Destructive actions are denied |
| `OC-08` | Denied action | Attempt a denied shell command | Blocked by policy |
| `OC-09` | Allowed action | Attempt an allowed command | Proceeds |
| `OC-10` | Secrets | Attempt to read `.env` | Denied |
| `OC-11` | External directory | Attempt to read outside the workspace | Denied |
| `OC-12` | Supply chain | Attempt an unapproved MCP, plugin, or skill | Denied |
| `OC-13` | Instructions | Read the instruction entries | `AGENTS.md` is loaded |
| `OC-14` | References | Read the reference list | All references are pinned |
| `OC-15` | Compaction | Read the compaction config | Enabled with a keep budget |
| `OC-16` | Sessions and worktrees | Create and remove a worktree | Both succeed |
| `OC-17` | Trace | Run a tool call and read the event stream | A tool event is emitted |
| `OC-18` | Stop | Interrupt a running session | The session stops |
| `OC-19` | Evidence | Produce and hash an evidence item | The hash is recorded |
| `OC-20` | Human handoff | Ask a question and answer it | The decision is recorded |
| `OC-21` | Model route | Run with a selected model | The route is in the trace |
| `OC-22` | Kill switch | Run the kill-switch drill | The run stops and credentials are revoked |
| `OC-23` | Version drift | Review the version and the changelog | The review is recorded |

## 4. Evidence

Record:

- the OpenCode version
- the commit and branch
- the command and output for each check
- the failures and the disposition
- the date and the assessor

A checklist without evidence is an opinion.

## 5. Result

A repository is OpenCode-conformant when every check passes or has a recorded,
time-bound exception. The result feeds the readiness assessment and the
conformance claim.

## 6. Anti-patterns

- Running the checklist against a different version than the one in use.
- Checking the config file without checking the effective permissions.
- Treating a `deny` policy as enough without a negative test.
- Testing in a sandbox that does not match the real deployment.
- A checklist with no evidence.
- A failed check marked as a warning.

# Readiness assessment

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

This is the question the whole specification exists to answer: what does this
repository lack for safe autonomy, and what should be fixed first? The
assessment scores 24 controls, computes the autonomy ceiling, and produces a
gap register with owners and remediation.

## 2. Principles

- Evidence-based: a control without evidence is unproven.
- Deterministic: the same repository and evidence produce the same score.
- No self-report: a claim in a document is not evidence.
- Weakest link: one unmet blocking control caps the ceiling.
- Independent: the assessor is read-only and separate from the implementer.
- Reassessed: a score expires when the repository or the policy changes.

## 3. Domains and controls

| ID | Domain | Question | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CTL-01` | Repository legibility | Is there a repository map, canonical commands, and a pinned toolchain? | `mise.toml`, README, clean-clone check |
| `CTL-02` | Work intake | Is there a work item with goal, acceptance criteria, risk tier, and evidence? | Work item schema and a real item |
| `CTL-03` | Ownership | Is there an owner and an escalation path? | `CODEOWNERS` or ownership table |
| `CTL-04` | Instructions | Is `AGENTS.md` current and consistent with `CONTRIBUTING.md`? | Instruction files and a link check |
| `CTL-05` | References and skills | Are references and skills pinned and reviewed? | Pins, review dates |
| `CTL-06` | Memory | Is compaction and durable memory governed? | Config, memory policy |
| `CTL-07` | Role contracts | Does every role have allowed and denied actions? | Role contracts |
| `CTL-08` | Least privilege | Are permissions and policies enforced by the runtime? | Config, negative tests |
| `CTL-09` | Identity and secrets | Is the agent identity separate, and are secrets denied? | Bot account, policy, trace |
| `CTL-10` | Policy red lines | Are destructive actions hard-denied? | Policy file and tests |
| `CTL-11` | Evidence manifest | Is the definition of done machine-readable? | Manifest and gate result |
| `CTL-12` | Decision rights | Is acceptance allocated by risk tier? | Decision matrix and records |
| `CTL-13` | Durable loop | Is state checkpointed and resumable? | Run state, resume test |
| `CTL-14` | Failure protocol | Is ambiguity blocked and failure classified? | Failure taxonomy, drill |
| `CTL-15` | Budgets and stop | Are budgets enforced and is the kill switch tested? | Limits, kill-switch drill |
| `CTL-16` | Concurrency | Are worktrees and ownership used? | Worktree record, lock policy |
| `CTL-17` | Merge queue | Is integration serialized and tested on the merged result? | Queue config, CI result |
| `CTL-18` | Rollback | Is there a tested rollback path? | Rollback plan and drill |
| `CTL-19` | Verification stack | Are the required checks layered and deterministic? | CI jobs, flake rate |
| `CTL-20` | Test integrity | Are mutation and test-diff guards enforced? | Mutation report, guard |
| `CTL-21` | Independent review | Is review separate and rubric-based? | Review record |
| `CTL-22` | Human acceptance | Is acceptance sampled by risk? | Acceptance record |
| `CTL-23` | Trace and provenance | Are trace and provenance complete and tamper-evident? | Trace export, hash chain |
| `CTL-24` | Metrics and evolution | Are health, evaluations, and incident drills in place? | Metrics, eval record, drill |

## 4. Scoring

| Score | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Absent: no artifact or practice |
| 1 | Manual: documented but ad hoc and human-dependent |
| 2 | Defined: documented, applied, and partly automated |
| 3 | Automated and evidenced: enforced by the runtime or CI, with current evidence and an audit sample |

Rules:

- A score requires evidence. Self-report is not evidence.
- Evidence must be current within the declared review window.
- A control with a missing prerequisite is capped at the prerequisite's score.
- The assessor records the evidence references, not only the number.
- A score of 3 requires at least one audit sample.

## 5. Gates and ceiling

| Level | Required controls |
| --- | --- |
| L1 | `CTL-01`-`CTL-04`, `CTL-07`, `CTL-08`, `CTL-10`-`CTL-14` at 2 or higher |
| L2 | L1 plus `CTL-05`, `CTL-06`, `CTL-09`, `CTL-15`-`CTL-17`, `CTL-19`, `CTL-21` at 2 or higher |
| L3 | L2 plus `CTL-20`, `CTL-22`, `CTL-23`, `CTL-24` at 3 or higher |
| L4 | L3 plus `CTL-15`, `CTL-16`, `CTL-17`, `CTL-23`, `CTL-24` at 3 or higher, and the incident and concurrency drills passed |

The assessment computes the ceiling:

1. Start at L4.
2. If any L4 gate is unmet, lower the ceiling to L3.
3. If any L3 gate is unmet, lower the ceiling to L2.
4. If any L2 gate is unmet, lower the ceiling to L1.
5. If any L1 gate is unmet, the ceiling is L0.
6. The highest level whose gates are all met is the ceiling.

The recommended level is the highest level supported by evidence. It is
normally equal to the ceiling; it is lower when a human owner chooses to run
below the ceiling.

## 6. Gap register

Every control below its required score produces a gap:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `controlID` | The control |
| `severity` | `blocker` if it caps the target level; `major` if it blocks the next level; `minor` otherwise |
| `finding` | What is missing |
| `remediation` | The smallest action that raises the score |
| `owner` | Who fixes it |
| `effort` | An estimate |

Sort the register by severity. Fix blockers first; a long list of minors does
not raise the ceiling while a blocker remains.

## 7. Assessment process

1. Collect the repository, commit, config, CI results, evidence, traces, and
   policies.
2. Verify that each artifact exists and is current.
3. Score each control with evidence references.
4. Check the gates.
5. Compute the ceiling.
6. Write the gap register.
7. Review the report with the owner.
8. Record the report.
9. Reassess after the remediation.

## 8. Assessor independence

- The assessor is read-only.
- The assessor uses a separate context from the implementer.
- An L3 or L4 claim needs a human review of the evidence.
- A promotion cannot rely on the implementer's self-assessment.
- The assessor declares conflicts of interest.

## 9. Reassessment

Reassess:

- after the remediation of a blocker
- quarterly
- after an incident
- after a model, provider, or policy change
- before an autonomy promotion

An expired report is not evidence.

## 10. Report

The report contains:

- repository, commit, time, and assessor
- profile and recommended level
- the ceiling
- the 24 control scores with evidence
- the gap register
- notes and limitations

## 11. Anti-patterns

- Self-report as evidence.
- Scoring from documentation only.
- Averaging scores instead of checking gates.
- Ignoring a blocker because the average is high.
- Stale evidence.
- An assessor with write access.
- A report with no owner.
- A promotion without a reassessment.

## 12. Data contract

- Schema: [schemas/readiness-report.schema.json](../../schemas/readiness-report.schema.json)
- Example: [examples/readiness-report.example.yaml](../../examples/readiness-report.example.yaml)

# CLI and automation contract

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

An implementation needs a stable surface. Scripts, CI, and other agents need
predictable output and exit codes. This document defines the command surface
that a Mycelia implementation must provide.

## 2. Principles

- Non-interactive by default in CI.
- Machine-readable output on stdout; human summaries are optional.
- Data to stdout; errors to stderr.
- Read-only commands never write.
- Write commands require an explicit confirmation or `--yes`.
- Every command is idempotent for the same inputs.
- No secrets in output.

## 3. Commands

| Command | Purpose | Writes | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mycelia init` | Copy the template and write `mycelia.yaml` | Yes | Files |
| `mycelia validate` | Validate configs, schemas, and examples | No | Validation result |
| `mycelia assess` | Run the readiness assessment | No | Readiness report |
| `mycelia plan` | Turn a work item into a plan | No | Plan |
| `mycelia run` | Execute the loop | Yes | Run state, trace, evidence |
| `mycelia verify` | Run the evidence manifest | Evidence | Evidence records |
| `mycelia report` | Build an audit or acceptance report | Optional | Report |
| `mycelia doctor` | Check the runtime and environment | No | Check result |
| `mycelia upgrade` | Diff and apply a template upgrade | Yes | Diff, migration |

## 4. Flags

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--config <path>` | Configuration file, default `mycelia.yaml` |
| `--format <format>` | Output format: json, yaml, or markdown; default markdown |
| `--out <path>` | Write the output to a file |
| `--profile <name>` | Override the profile |
| `--risk <R0-R4>` | Override the risk tier |
| `--agent <id>` | Select the role |
| `--model <provider/model#variant>` | Select the model |
| `--max-cost <usd>` | Cost limit |
| `--max-tokens <n>` | Token limit |
| `--max-steps <n>` | Step limit |
| `--dry-run` | Print the actions without writing |
| `--yes` | Confirm a write command |
| `--quiet` | Suppress the human summary |
| `--verbose` | Add diagnostic output |

## 5. Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success |
| `1` | Policy violation |
| `2` | Invalid input, config, or schema |
| `3` | Blocked; a human decision is required |
| `4` | Budget exhausted |
| `5` | Internal error |
| `6` | Conformance failure |

A blocked run exits `3`, never `0`. A policy denial exits `1`, never `0`.

## 6. Output

- JSON and YAML output must validate against the matching schema:
  readiness, run state, evidence, review, acceptance, release, incident,
  trace, provenance, or evaluation.
- Markdown output is a human summary; scripts must not parse it.
- Errors include a code, a message, and a remediation hint.
- No secret, token, or personal data in the output.
- `--format json` is the CI default.

## 7. Safety and idempotency

- `init`, `validate`, `assess`, `plan`, and `doctor` are read-only.
- `run` requires `--yes` for a non-interactive write.
- `run --dry-run` prints the planned actions and exits `0`.
- `run` requires a clean worktree or `--worktree`.
- `run` never pushes to `main` and never merges by default.
- The same work item, commit, and action returns the same result.
- A retry does not duplicate a branch, pull request, evidence item, or release.

## 8. OpenCode mapping

| Command | OpenCode mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| `run` | `opencode run --format json --agent --model --worktree` |
| `assess` | Read-only session with the assessor agent |
| `plan` | Read-only session with the planner agent |
| `verify` | Verifier session with the allowed test commands |
| `report` | Read the trace, evidence, and run state |
| `doctor` | `opencode --version`, config validation, API check |

## 9. Examples

```sh
mycelia validate
mycelia assess --format json --out readiness.json
mycelia plan --work-item MYC-123 --format markdown
mycelia run --work-item MYC-123 --dry-run
mycelia run --work-item MYC-123 --yes --max-cost 20
mycelia verify --work-item MYC-123 --commit abc1234
mycelia report --run RUN-001 --format markdown
mycelia doctor
```

## 10. Anti-patterns

- Interactive prompts in CI.
- Human-readable output parsed by scripts.
- Exit `0` on a blocked or denied run.
- A destructive default.
- Hidden network calls.
- Secrets in output.
- Non-idempotent retries.
- A command that writes during `validate` or `assess`.

# File formats

Status: Draft

## 1. Purpose

An implementation and an adopter need to know where each artifact lives, what
format it uses, and how it is validated. This document defines the repository
layout and the schema index.

## 2. Root layout

```text
mycelia.yaml              # factory configuration
opencode.json             # OpenCode runtime configuration
AGENTS.md                 # operating contract
CONTRIBUTING.md           # human contribution guide
schemas/                  # JSON Schemas
examples/                 # validated examples
docs/                     # normative specification
.opencode/
  agents/                 # role definitions
  commands/               # prompt templates
  skills/                 # procedural knowledge
  plugins/                # optional, reviewed
runs/                     # generated run state (not committed by default)
evidence/                 # generated or external evidence
trace/                    # generated trace export
readiness/                # generated readiness reports
```

## 3. Formats

| Artifact | Format | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Factory configuration | YAML | Human-authored, comments, multi-line |
| Runtime configuration | JSON | Validated against the OpenCode schema |
| Schemas | JSON Schema 2020-12 | Tooling and validation |
| Records | YAML | Human-readable audit records |
| Trace | JSONL | Append-only event stream |
| Specifications | Markdown | Reviewable, lintable |
| Machine output | JSON | Scriptable |
| Human summary | Markdown | Readable |

## 4. Naming and IDs

| Artifact | Pattern | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work item | `MYC-<n>` | `MYC-123` |
| Run | `RUN-<n>` | `RUN-001` |
| Evidence | `EVD-<TYPE>-<n>` | `EVD-LINT-001` |
| Manifest | `EM-<n>` | `EM-001` |
| Policy decision | `PD-<n>` | `PD-001` |
| Review | `REV-<n>` | `REV-001` |
| Acceptance | `ACC-<n>` | `ACC-001` |
| Release | `REL-<n>` | `REL-001` |
| Trace event | `EVT-<TYPE>-<n>` | `EVT-TOOL-001` |
| Provenance | `PRV-<n>` | `PRV-001` |
| Evaluation | `EVA-<n>` | `EVA-001` |
| Incident | `INC-<n>` | `INC-001` |
| Readiness | `RPT-<n>` | `RPT-001` |
| Handoff | `HND-<n>` | `HND-001` |
| Test integrity | `TIR-<n>` | `TIR-001` |

File names use lower-case kebab-case. Agent, command, and skill IDs use

## 6. Validation

```sh
mise run lint:schemas
```

The task:

1. validates every schema against the 2020-12 meta-schema;
2. validates every example against its schema.

A new schema updates:

- the file in `schemas/`
- the example in `examples/`
- `schemas/README.md`
- `mise.toml` and the CI job
- the traceability matrix

## 7. Versioning

- Every document and record uses `apiVersion: mycelia/v1`.
- Schema `$id` values are stable.
- An additive optional field can stay in v1.
- A required field, a removal, or a semantic change needs a new major version.
- A deprecated field is documented for at least one minor release.

## 8. Committed, generated, or ephemeral

| Artifact | Committed | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Specs, schemas, examples, configs | Yes | Source of truth |
| Agents, commands, skills | Yes | Reviewed |
| Run state | No by default | Generated; commit a sample if needed |
| Evidence artifacts | No by default | External store; hash in trace |
| Trace | No by default | External sink; export on request |
| Readiness report | Optional | Commit for an audit snapshot |
| Review, acceptance, release, incident records | Optional | Commit the decision record |

Large artifacts stay external; the hash is the durable reference.

## 9. Anti-patterns

- A YAML file without a schema.
- A schema without an example.
- A committed trace with secrets.
- A generated file that looks editable.
- A file name that encodes a version.
- An `apiVersion` that drifts between documents.
- A schema change with no example update.
